/landing-3d.answer: Diagramwise is a system design practice tool. You pick a realistic problem, build the architecture on a visual canvas, explain your assumptions and trade-offs, and receive structured feedback on scalability, reliability, and data design so you can improve the next iteration.

faqs.q: What is Diagramwise?
faqs.a: Diagramwise is a web-based system design practice environment. It combines an interactive architecture canvas with realistic problems, learning paths, and structured design review.

faqs.q: Who is Diagramwise for?
faqs.a: It is built for engineers preparing for system design interviews, developers learning distributed systems, and teams who want to document and review architecture decisions.

faqs.q: How does the architecture review work?
faqs.a: You build a diagram and write down your requirements, assumptions, and trade-offs. Diagramwise then reviews the design for scalability, reliability, data design, and trade-offs, and points out strengths, risks, and practical improvements.

faqs.q: Which cloud and diagram components are supported?
faqs.a: The canvas includes generic architecture components plus AWS, Azure, and GCP components, along with UML and entity-relationship diagram shapes.

faqs.q: Is Diagramwise free?
faqs.a: Diagramwise is free with usage limits. You can open the design studio, browse practice problems and learning paths, and build diagrams without paying. Features that cost money to run, such as AI feedback, have usage limits. Paid plans may be added later, and any change will be announced first.

/problems.answer: Practice problems are realistic system design and AI/ML architecture challenges. Each one lists requirements and scale assumptions, then lets you build the architecture on an interactive canvas and get feedback on the decisions behind your design.

faqs.q: What kinds of system design problems are available?
faqs.a: Problems cover distributed systems, infrastructure such as caching, queues and search, product applications such as URL shorteners and ride sharing, and AI and ML systems including RAG, inference, and MLOps.

faqs.q: How should I choose a system design problem?
faqs.a: Pick one narrow prompt that isolates the skill you want to improve, such as caching or consistency, rather than jumping between unrelated problems.

faqs.q: What does each problem include?
faqs.a: Each problem has an interview prompt, functional and non-functional requirements, scale assumptions, key entities, a data flow, and deep dives on trade-offs.

/system-design-interview.answerQuestion: How do you prepare for a system design interview?
/system-design-interview.answer: Prepare by practicing a repeatable method: clarify requirements, estimate traffic and storage, draw the simplest end-to-end flow, defend each trade-off, then test failure and scale. Practicing on concrete problems with a diagram builds the fluency interviewers look for.

faqs.q: What is a system design interview?
faqs.a: It is an interview where you design a large-scale system, such as a URL shortener or notification service, from an ambiguous prompt. Interviewers assess how you handle requirements, scale, trade-offs, and failure.

faqs.q: What steps should I follow in a system design interview?
faqs.a: Clarify the problem and non-goals, estimate scale, sketch the critical request path, deepen the riskiest components, and finish by walking through failure modes and consistency.

faqs.q: How long should I prepare for a system design interview?
faqs.a: It depends on your starting point, but steady practice on a handful of well-chosen problems, reviewed for weaknesses and repeated, beats reading many solutions passively.

faqs.q: Do I need to draw diagrams in the interview?
faqs.a: Yes. A clear diagram of components and data flow makes your reasoning easy to follow and gives the interviewer something concrete to probe.

sections.heading: What interviewers actually evaluate
paragraphs: A system design interview is not a quiz with one correct diagram. The interviewer is watching how you handle an ambiguous problem: whether you ask questions before building, whether your numbers drive your choices, and whether you can explain what each decision costs.
Most rubrics reduce to five signals. Strong candidates show all five, even when their final architecture is ordinary.
bullets: Problem framing: you turn a vague prompt into explicit requirements, non-goals, and success criteria.
Scale reasoning: you estimate traffic, storage, and latency, and let those numbers justify your choices.
Architecture: you produce a coherent end-to-end design with clear component boundaries.
Trade-offs: you name the alternatives you rejected and why.
Resilience: you describe what breaks, how you would notice, and how the system recovers.

sections.heading: A 45-minute time budget
paragraphs: Candidates most often fail by spending the whole hour on one component. A rough budget keeps the conversation balanced. Treat these numbers as a starting point and adjust if the interviewer steers you elsewhere.

rows: Critical path diagram and main components
Data model, one or two hard components in detail
Summary, trade-offs, what you would build next

sections.heading: Step 1: clarify before you draw
paragraphs: The first minutes decide the rest of the interview. Ask questions that change the design, not questions that sound thorough. A useful test is whether a different answer would produce a different architecture.
bullets: Who are the users, and what are the two or three core use cases?
What is explicitly out of scope? Naming non-goals protects your time.
What is the expected scale: users, requests per day, data size, growth?
Is the workload read-heavy or write-heavy, and what is the read-to-write ratio?
What latency matters, and for which operations?
Is strong consistency required, or is eventual consistency acceptable?
What availability target is expected, and what is the cost of downtime?
paragraphs_after: Write the answers on the board. They become the contract you check your design against at the end.

sections.heading: Step 2: estimate the numbers you need
paragraphs: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is about orders of magnitude, not precision. The goal is to learn whether you are designing for tens, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of requests per second, because that changes whether you need a cache, sharding, or a queue.

A day has about 86,400 seconds, so it is convenient to round to roughly 100,000. Divide daily volume by that to get average requests per second, then multiply by a peak factor, commonly between 2 and 10 depending on how bursty the traffic is.
paragraphs_after: Storage works the same way: records per day, times bytes per record, times retention. A service that stores 1 KB per record and receives 100 million records a day writes about 100 GB per day, or roughly 36 TB per year before replication.

It also helps to remember rough latency orders of magnitude. These are approximations that vary by hardware, but the ratios are what matter: a memory access is around 100 nanoseconds, a random read from an SSD is roughly 100 microseconds, a round trip inside one data center is around half a millisecond, a spinning disk seek is on the order of 10 milliseconds, and a cross-continent network round trip is around 150 milliseconds. The lesson is that a network hop costs far more than a memory access, and a cross-region call costs far more than a local one.

sections.heading: Step 3: draw the critical path first
paragraphs: Start with the simplest flow that satisfies the main use case: a client, a load balancer, a stateless service, and a data store. Only after that works end to end should you add components, and each addition should be motivated by a number or a requirement you already stated.
Common building blocks and the problem each one solves:
bullets: Cache: reduces read latency and database load for data that is read far more often than it changes.
Message queue: decouples producers from consumers, absorbs bursts, and lets slow work happen asynchronously.
CDN: serves static or cacheable content close to users and offloads origin traffic.
Read replicas: scale read throughput, at the cost of replication lag.
Sharding or partitioning: scales writes and storage beyond one machine, at the cost of cross-shard queries and rebalancing.
Search index: supports text and multi-field queries that a primary database handles poorly.

sections.heading: Step 4: state the trade-off out loud
paragraphs: Every component choice trades one property for another. Interviewers listen for the sentence "I chose X over Y because...". If you cannot say what you gave up, you probably have not made a decision yet.

rows: Cost of showing stale data to a user
Whether the user must wait for the result
Read/write ratio and tolerance for stale entries
Current headroom and how fast load grows

sections.heading: Step 5: test failure and scale
paragraphs: Finish by walking your own design through the ways it can fail. This is where average answers become strong ones, because it shows you think about the system after launch, not just on the whiteboard.
Questions worth asking about your own diagram:
bullets: What is the single point of failure, and how would you remove it?
What happens when a dependency is slow rather than down? Timeouts, retries with exponential backoff, and circuit breakers prevent a slow service from taking everything else with it.
Are retried operations idempotent? A retried payment or message must not be applied twice.
Where can one hot key or hot partition overload a single node?
How stale can a read replica or cache get, and is that acceptable?
How will you know something is wrong: which metrics, logs, and alerts exist?

sections.heading: A worked estimate: a URL shortener
paragraphs: Suppose the prompt is a URL shortener and you agree on 100 million new links per month with ten reads for every write.

Writes: 100 million per month is about 3.3 million per day, or roughly 40 writes per second on average. Reads: ten times that, about 400 per second on average, perhaps 1,200 at peak. This is a modest load, which tells you a single well-indexed database with a cache in front can carry it, and you do not need to shard on day one.

Storage: if you keep each link for five years, that is about 6 billion records. At roughly 500 bytes each, that is about 3 TB before replication, which fits on one modern database server but is large enough that you should plan for partitioning later.

Key length: a seven-character key using 62 characters (a to z, A to Z, 0 to 9) has about 3.5 trillion combinations, far more than the 6 billion you need, so seven characters is comfortable. Notice how each number drove a concrete decision.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Drawing components before agreeing on requirements, then discovering the design does not fit the problem.
Skipping estimation, so every choice is a guess and no choice can be defended.
Over-engineering: designing for global scale when the prompt describes ten thousand users.
Listing technologies instead of explaining why: naming Kafka or Cassandra is not a decision.
Never stating a trade-off, or presenting a choice as if it had no downside.
Ignoring failure until the interviewer asks about it.
Treating the interview as a monologue. The interviewer's hints are information; follow them.

sections.heading: How to practice
paragraphs: Reading solutions builds recognition, but the interview tests recall under pressure. The reliable way to improve is to solve problems yourself, review your own gaps, and repeat the weak area.

Pick one problem below, set a 45-minute timer, and follow the five steps without looking at a reference. Then review which step was weakest, such as estimation or failure handling, and choose your next problem to exercise that step.

/system-design-practice.answerQuestion: How do you practice system design online?
/system-design-practice.answer: Choose one narrow prompt, time-box requirements and assumptions, build and annotate the architecture, review it for weaknesses, then repeat the dimension you missed. Diagramwise provides the canvas, realistic prompts, and structured review to run this practice loop.

faqs.q: How can I practice system design on my own?
faqs.a: Pick a problem, write requirements first, draw the architecture, explain why each component exists, and review the result before changing the diagram.

faqs.q: What is deliberate practice in system design?
faqs.a: It means isolating one skill, such as caching or database scaling, getting feedback on it, and repeating until the weakness disappears, instead of only solving new problems.

faqs.q: How do I know my design is good?
faqs.a: A good design meets the stated requirements, makes its trade-offs explicit, and survives walkthroughs of overload, partial failure, and recovery.

sections.heading: Why reading solutions is not enough
paragraphs: Reading a finished design builds recognition: you see a diagram and think it looks right. An interview, and real design work, tests recall. You start from a blank page, an ambiguous prompt, and a clock. The gap between those two skills is why people who have read many solutions still freeze on the first question.

Deliberate practice closes that gap. It means working on one specific skill, producing your own answer before looking at anyone else's, getting concrete feedback, and repeating the weak area until it stops being weak.

sections.heading: Pick one narrow skill per session
paragraphs: The most common practice mistake is choosing the largest, most famous problem every time. A problem that touches ten concerns gives you feedback on none of them. Instead, choose a prompt that isolates the skill you want to improve, then match it to a problem.

headers: What the problem forces you to decide
rows: What to cache, where, for how long, and how stale entries are handled (a distributed cache)
Algorithm choice, shared counters, behavior under burst (an API rate limiter)
Queues, retries, delivery guarantees, fan-out (a notification system)
Exactly-once versus at-least-once, leases, recovery (a job scheduler)
Preventing double booking and handling concurrent updates (a hotel booking system)
Retries, duplicate requests, reconciliation (a payment system)

sections.heading: A 60-minute practice session
paragraphs: A fixed structure keeps sessions comparable, so you can tell whether you are actually improving. This is a workable template; shorten or lengthen the blocks to fit your schedule.

rows: Read once, then close any reference material
Functional requirements, non-goals, scale assumptions, success criteria
Draw the architecture and label each flow and component with why it exists
Check the design against your own requirements and the checklist below, writing down weaknesses without fixing them yet
Change the design to address the single most important weakness

paragraphs_after: Writing down weaknesses before editing the diagram matters. If you fix problems as you notice them, you never see which kinds of mistakes you repeat.

sections.heading: A self-review checklist
paragraphs: After building, review your own design before comparing it with any reference. Ask these questions about each major component and flow:
bullets: Does every component trace back to a stated requirement or a number you estimated?
Can I explain what this component costs, such as latency, consistency, operational burden, or money?
What is the single point of failure, and what happens when it fails?
Where does the data live, which copy is the source of truth, and how do the others stay in sync?
What happens at ten times the assumed load? Which part breaks first?
Is each operation safe to retry, or can a retry cause a duplicate effect?
How would I notice that this is broken in production?

sections.heading: Keep a decision log
paragraphs: A diagram records what you built. A decision log records why, which is the part interviewers and teammates actually test. For each significant choice, write four short lines:
bullets: Decision: what you chose.
Alternatives: what you considered and rejected.
Reason and cost: why you chose it and what it gives up.
Revisit when: the condition, such as a scale threshold, that would change the decision.
paragraphs_after: Reading your own log a week later is one of the fastest ways to spot shallow reasoning, such as decisions that have no stated alternative or no stated cost.

sections.heading: A four-week plan
paragraphs: If you have a month, group practice by theme rather than by company or product. Each week deepens one layer, and the final week combines them under time pressure.

rows: Requirements, back-of-the-envelope estimation, single server to a load-balanced service
Storage choices, caching, replication, partitioning, consistency
Queues, retries, idempotency, failure modes, observability
Full problems under a timer, followed by a written review of recurring weaknesses

sections.heading: Common mistakes in practice
bullets: Memorizing diagrams. A memorized answer collapses as soon as the interviewer changes one requirement.
Always practicing the same famous problem and never the ones that expose your gaps.
Skipping the review step, so each session repeats the last session's mistakes.
Practicing only the area you already enjoy, such as drawing boxes, and avoiding estimation or failure analysis.
Never timing yourself, then running out of time in the real interview.
Practicing silently. Explaining your reasoning out loud, or to another person, is a separate skill that needs its own repetition.

sections.heading: How to tell you are improving
paragraphs: Progress in system design is easy to feel and hard to measure, so use concrete signals. You can produce a usable estimate in about five minutes. You can name at least two trade-offs for each major component without prompting. You find your own weaknesses during review instead of discovering them later.
One of the most useful tests is to repeat a problem two weeks later without looking at your earlier answer. If the second attempt is clearer, better justified, and faster, the practice is working.

sections.heading: Practice with another person
paragraphs: Solo practice builds the design skill, but a partner builds the conversation skill. Ask someone to play the interviewer: they give the prompt, answer clarifying questions, and push back on one decision. Even a friend who is not a system design expert can ask why you chose something, which forces you to articulate reasoning you may have only half formed.
When no partner is available, record yourself explaining the design and listen for places where you skip a reason or hedge a decision.

/ai-system-design-interview.answerQuestion: What is an AI system design interview?
/ai-system-design-interview.answer: An AI system design interview asks you to design a machine learning or LLM-powered product end to end. You separate offline data and training paths from online inference, budget latency, quality and cost, and plan evaluation, monitoring, and graceful degradation when a model fails.

faqs.q: How is AI system design different from classic system design?
faqs.a: You still design for scale and reliability, but you also reason about data quality, model evaluation, drift, inference latency and cost, and fallbacks when the model is wrong or unavailable.

faqs.q: What topics come up in AI and ML system design interviews?
faqs.a: Common topics are data pipelines, feature stores, retrieval and RAG, model serving, evaluation, monitoring, and cost control.

faqs.q: How should I structure an ML system design answer?
faqs.a: Define the product behavior and quality metric, show the offline and online paths, budget latency and cost, then cover evaluation, observability, and rollback.

sections.heading: How AI system design differs from classic system design
paragraphs: A classic design question asks you to build a deterministic system that scales. An AI design question keeps all of that and adds three things: the output is probabilistic, the quality depends on data that keeps changing, and the most expensive component, the model, behaves differently from ordinary services.

That means a complete answer covers more than boxes and arrows. You need a definition of quality, a path for data and models to be updated safely, a budget for latency and cost, and a plan for the moments when the model is wrong or unavailable.

sections.heading: Separate the offline path from the online path
paragraphs: The single most useful structure for any ML or LLM design is to split it into two flows that run on different schedules and have different requirements.
bullets: Offline path: data ingestion, cleaning, labeling, feature computation, training or index building, evaluation, and registering a versioned model or index artifact. It is throughput-oriented and can take minutes to days.

Online path: receiving a request, retrieving features or context, running inference, post-processing, returning a response, and logging inputs and outputs for feedback. It is latency-oriented and must respond in milliseconds to seconds.
paragraphs_after: Draw both, and draw the feedback loop that connects them: logged predictions and user outcomes flow back into the offline path as new training and evaluation data. Interviewers often probe whether you remembered that loop.

sections.heading: Define quality before you design
paragraphs: Ask what the model must produce and how anyone will know it is good. Without a metric, every architecture choice is unfalsifiable. Distinguish offline metrics, measured on a held-out evaluation set before release, from online metrics, measured on real traffic, usually through an A/B test.
Examples of how the metric depends on the product:

rows: Precision, recall, F1 at a chosen threshold
p95 latency, error rate, cost per prediction
Recall at k, mean reciprocal rank, NDCG
p95 latency, index freshness, cost per query
NDCG offline, click-through or conversion online
p95 latency, coverage, cost per request
Task success rate, groundedness against sources, human ratings
Time to first token, tokens per request, cost per request

sections.heading: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) design
paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model in your own documents. The offline path splits documents into chunks, converts each chunk into an embedding vector, and stores the vectors in an index. The online path embeds the user's question, retrieves the most similar chunks, optionally reranks them, places them in the prompt, and asks the model to answer using that context, ideally with citations.
Each step contains a trade-off worth naming:
bullets: Chunk size: small chunks are precise but lose context; large chunks keep context but dilute relevance and use more of the prompt.
Number of retrieved chunks: more chunks raise recall but increase cost, latency, and the chance of distracting the model.
Reranking: a second, more accurate model improves ordering at the price of extra latency and compute.
Hybrid search: combining keyword search with vector search often handles exact terms, such as product codes, better than vectors alone.
Freshness: decide how quickly changed documents must appear in the index, and design incremental re-indexing rather than rebuilding everything.

sections.heading: Budget latency, quality, and cost together
paragraphs: In most AI products the model call dominates both latency and cost, so the design question becomes where you can avoid, shrink, or hide it. Name the lever and its price:

rows: Latency and cost for repeated or similar requests
Possible drop in quality on hard cases
More complex client and error handling
Removes the model from the user's wait
Only works when the result is not needed immediately

sections.heading: Evaluate before release and monitor after
paragraphs: Model quality changes after launch because the world changes. Input data drifts, user behavior shifts, and upstream pipelines break silently. A strong design treats evaluation as an ongoing system, not a one-time test.

Before release, run the candidate against a fixed evaluation set and compare it with the current model. Release gradually, using shadow mode to run it without serving its output, then a canary on a small share of traffic, then a wider A/B test.
bullets: Monitor input distributions to detect data drift.
Sample and review outputs, using automated checks and human review, to catch quality regressions.
Track operational metrics: latency percentiles, error rates, token or compute usage, and cost.
Log enough to reproduce a bad answer: the model version, the retrieved context, and the prompt.

sections.heading: Plan for degradation and rollback
paragraphs: Interviewers like to ask what happens when the model, the vector index, the feature store, or a third-party provider is unavailable. Have an answer for each, in order from best to worst experience.
bullets: Fall back to a smaller model, a cached answer, or a simple rule-based or keyword result.
Return a clear partial result or an honest error instead of a confident wrong answer.
Keep previous model and index versions deployed so you can roll back quickly, and make the switch a configuration change.
Provide a kill switch for a misbehaving feature, and a human review path where mistakes are costly.

sections.heading: Safety, privacy, and access control
paragraphs: Production AI systems need a few non-negotiable controls, and mentioning them signals maturity. Apply access control before retrieval, so a user can only receive context from documents they are permitted to see; filtering afterward risks leaking restricted content into the prompt.

Treat retrieved text and user input as untrusted. A document or web page can contain instructions that try to hijack the model, a risk called prompt injection, so keep untrusted content separated from system instructions and limit what actions the model can trigger. Minimize and mask personal data in logs and training sets, and define retention rules.

sections.heading: A worked estimate: semantic search
paragraphs: Suppose the prompt is a semantic search over one million support articles, using 768-dimensional embeddings stored as 32-bit floats.

Each vector is 768 times 4 bytes, which is 3,072 bytes. One million vectors is about 3 GB of raw vector data. Indexes add overhead, so plan for a few multiples of that, but the result is small enough to hold in memory on a single node. At 50 queries per second, a replicated pair of index nodes is comfortable, and the model that creates query embeddings is likely the larger latency cost than the vector lookup itself.

The numbers lead directly to design decisions: no sharding is needed at this size, replication is for availability rather than capacity, and the effort belongs in chunking, reranking, and evaluation quality rather than infrastructure.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Designing only the serving path and forgetting how data and models are produced and updated.
Never defining a quality metric, so no design can be judged better or worse.
Ignoring cost. A design that is accurate but costs too much per request is not viable.
No fallback, so a model outage becomes a full product outage.
Evaluating once at launch and never monitoring drift afterward.
Putting user data in prompts or logs without considering privacy and access control.

/kubernetes-architecture.answer: Kubernetes architecture splits a cluster into a control plane and worker nodes. The control plane, made of the API server, scheduler, controllers, and etcd, reconciles declared state, while nodes run Pods behind Services and Ingress with storage, configuration, and observability around them.

faqs.q: What are the main components of Kubernetes?
faqs.a: The control plane has the API server, scheduler, controller manager, and etcd. Each worker node runs a kubelet, a container runtime, and a network proxy, and hosts Pods.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet?
faqs.a: A Deployment manages interchangeable stateless Pods. A StatefulSet gives Pods stable identities and storage, which suits databases and other stateful workloads.

faqs.q: How does traffic reach a Pod in Kubernetes?
faqs.a: External traffic typically enters through an Ingress, is routed to a Service, and is load-balanced across the matching Pods, with network policies controlling what may connect.

faqs.q: How do I draw a Kubernetes architecture diagram?
faqs.a: Show the workload boundary, the traffic path from Ingress to Pods, the control plane, persistent storage, and the operational pieces such as scaling and observability.

sections.heading: The two halves of a cluster
paragraphs: A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane that decides what should run, and worker nodes that run it. The control plane stores the desired state of the cluster and continuously works to make reality match it. Nodes host the Pods, which are the smallest deployable units and contain one or more containers.

A clear architecture diagram separates these two halves, because they fail differently and are operated differently. Application traffic flows through the nodes; configuration and orchestration flow through the control plane.

rows: The front end of the cluster. Every other component talks to the cluster through it, and it is the only component that reads and writes etcd.
A consistent, highly available key-value store holding all cluster state.
Watches for new Pods with no node and assigns each to a suitable node.
Runs the controllers that move current state toward desired state, such as the Deployment and Node controllers.
Integrates with a cloud provider for resources such as load balancers and node lifecycle.
Makes sure the containers described in assigned Pods are running and healthy.
Actually runs containers, for example containerd or CRI-O.
Implements Service networking rules so traffic reaches the right Pods.

sections.heading: The reconciliation loop
paragraphs: The idea that explains most Kubernetes behavior is reconciliation. You declare a desired state, for example three replicas of a service. The API server stores it in etcd. Controllers observe the difference between the desired and the current state and act to close it: creating Pods, replacing failed ones, or scaling up. The scheduler places new Pods on nodes, and each node's kubelet starts the containers.

This is why a diagram should show the control plane as a set of loops reacting to declared state, not as a request path. When a node dies, no one tells Kubernetes what to do; the controllers notice the missing Pods and create replacements.

sections.heading: Choose the workload type deliberately
paragraphs: Picking the wrong controller is a frequent source of design problems. Match the workload type to how the application runs and stores state.

rows: Interchangeable Pods with rolling updates and rollbacks
Stable network identity and per-Pod persistent storage
Node-level agents such as log or metrics collectors
One Pod on every matching node
Runs to completion and retries on failure

sections.heading: Make the traffic path explicit
paragraphs: Every Pod gets its own IP address, but Pods are ephemeral, so clients should not depend on those addresses. A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances across the healthy Pods selected by its labels. Common Service types are ClusterIP for internal traffic, NodePort, and LoadBalancer for external exposure through a cloud load balancer.

For HTTP traffic from outside the cluster, an Ingress, or the newer Gateway API, defines routing rules by host and path. These rules only take effect if an ingress controller is running in the cluster. In a diagram, trace one request: client, load balancer, ingress, Service, Pod, and then any downstream data store.

Network policies restrict which Pods can talk to which. They are enforced only if the cluster's network plugin supports them, so state that assumption. By default, all Pods can reach all other Pods, which is rarely what you want in production.

sections.heading: State, configuration, and secrets
bullets: Persistent storage: a PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage, a StorageClass describes how it is provisioned, and a PersistentVolume is the underlying volume. Decide the backup and recovery boundary explicitly.
Configuration: use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive settings so the same image runs in every environment.
Secrets: they hold credentials, but by default they are only base64-encoded, not encrypted. Enable encryption at rest for etcd, restrict access with RBAC, and consider an external secret manager.
paragraphs_after: A useful design question is whether a stateful system belongs in the cluster at all. Running a database in Kubernetes is possible with a StatefulSet and the right operator, but a managed database service often removes significant operational work.

sections.heading: Design for scaling and availability
paragraphs: Availability in Kubernetes is the result of several small settings working together, so a good design names them.
bullets: Resource requests and limits: requests drive scheduling decisions and limits cap usage. Without requests, the scheduler cannot place Pods sensibly.
Readiness and liveness probes: a readiness probe keeps traffic away from a Pod that is not ready; a liveness probe restarts a stuck container. They answer different questions and are easy to confuse.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adjusts the number of replicas based on metrics such as CPU. Scaling nodes is a separate mechanism, so a diagram that shows Pods scaling should also show how nodes scale.
PodDisruptionBudget: limits how many replicas can be down during voluntary disruptions such as node drains.
Rolling updates: control how many Pods are replaced at a time so a deployment does not remove capacity all at once.
Spreading replicas: use topology spread constraints or anti-affinity so replicas land on different nodes and zones.

sections.heading: Security basics to include
paragraphs: A diagram that ignores security is incomplete. At minimum, show role-based access control with least-privilege service accounts, network policies limiting Pod-to-Pod traffic, Pod security settings that avoid running as root or with extra privileges, and a trusted image source with pinned versions rather than the mutable latest tag.
For managed clusters, note which responsibilities belong to the provider, such as the control plane, and which belong to you, such as node configuration, workloads, and access policies.

sections.heading: Observability and operations
paragraphs: Operations is a first-class part of the architecture. Include a metrics pipeline for cluster and application metrics, centralized logging, and alerts on symptoms that users feel, such as error rate and latency, as well as on cluster health, such as failing nodes and Pods stuck in a pending or crash-looping state.
Also state your rollout and rollback strategy. Kubernetes can roll a Deployment back to a previous revision, but that only helps if your changes are backward compatible with the data they touch.

rows: Operational capacity versus need for control

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Omitting resource requests and limits, which makes scheduling unpredictable and lets one workload starve others.
Skipping readiness probes, so traffic reaches Pods that cannot serve it yet.
Running a single replica and calling it highly available.
Treating Pods as durable. Anything written to a container filesystem is lost when the Pod is replaced.
Assuming Secrets are encrypted by default, or granting broad RBAC permissions out of convenience.
Using the latest image tag, which makes deployments and rollbacks unpredictable.
On self-managed clusters, running etcd without backups or a tested restore.

sections.heading: A checklist for your diagram
paragraphs: Before you call a Kubernetes diagram finished, check that it shows the workload type and why it was chosen, the full request path from client to Pod, the control plane and what it reconciles, where state is stored and how it is recovered, how configuration and secrets are delivered, how the system scales and tolerates node failure, and how you would observe and roll it back. For definitive details on any component, consult the official Kubernetes documentation.

/about.answer: Diagramwise is a product of Next Zen, a studio that builds developer tools for learning algorithms, designing system architecture, and automating cloud infrastructure. It is built and maintained by Next Zen, and its source code is on GitHub.

faqs.q: Who makes Diagramwise?
faqs.a: Diagramwise is made by Next Zen, which also builds Learn Algo and Orchestrator.

faqs.q: What does Diagramwise do?
faqs.a: It lets you practice system design by building architectures on a visual canvas, explaining your trade-offs, and getting structured feedback on scalability, reliability, and data design.

faqs.q: Is Diagramwise free?
faqs.a: Diagramwise is free with usage limits. You can open the design studio, browse practice problems and learning paths, and build diagrams without paying. Features that cost money to run, such as AI feedback, have usage limits. Paid plans may be added later, and any change will be announced first.

faqs.q: What else does Next Zen build?
faqs.a: Learn Algo teaches algorithms visually, from data structures to machine learning, and Orchestrator lets you design cloud infrastructure visually and generate Terraform.

faqs.q: How can I report a bug or ask a question?
faqs.a: Use the Send feedback option on this page, or the Feedback button in the corner of the app, to report a bug, ask a question, or suggest an improvement. You can also open an issue in the GitHub repository at github.com/satya00089/diagrammatic.
